title: Your BFCM marketing stack is changing. Is your privacy setup keeping up?
summary: BFCM prep often adds new tags, apps, and vendors to your stack. Here’s how to check whether your consent setup, privacy disclosures, and request workflows still match how your store runs today.
body_markdown:
The focus is on making sure everything works when traffic picks up. Campaigns need to launch on time, pixels need to capture the right information, and reporting needs to be reliable.


But those changes can also affect how customer data is collected, shared, and managed. A new tracking pixel might need to be accounted for in your consent setup. A storefront update could change how existing scripts behave.


Your privacy setup may have worked as intended a few months ago. The question is whether it still reflects how your business operates today.


## Your BFCM stack probably looks different than it did a month ago


BFCM tends to compress months of website and marketing changes into a few busy weeks. Teams are launching campaigns, testing promotions, and making last-minute adjustments to improve conversion rates before traffic spikes.


An agency might add an advertising integration through Google Tag Manager (GTM). Your ecommerce team might install a Shopify app for upselling or launch a seasonal theme. Marketing might introduce a personalization tool that shares customer information with another vendor.


Each change makes sense on its own, and everyone is focused on getting their part of the launch ready.


The challenge is that privacy responsibilities often sit across those same teams.


Your agency may know exactly which tags were added but have limited visibility into how consent is configured. Your developer may know which scripts are running without knowing whether a new vendor needs to be reflected in your privacy policy. And whoever manages consumer privacy requests may never hear about the new app collecting customer information.


It's how a series of routine updates can leave your privacy setup reflecting an earlier version of your business.


## Every change can affect more than the campaign


Consider something as routine as adding a new retargeting pixel. Marketing wants to reach shoppers who visited the site but didn't purchase, so the team adds the integration and confirms it's collecting data.


But there's more to consider. What customer information does the pixel collect? When does it fire? Does it respond appropriately to visitors' consent or opt-out choices? And does the integration introduce a new vendor or data use that needs to be documented?


These questions matter for privacy compliance, but they can also affect the marketing work you're trying to accomplish.


For example, a consent banner might still appear and function as expected while a newly added tag isn't configured to respond to visitors' choices. Depending on the implementation, tracking may also behave differently across visitors, affecting the data available for campaign reporting and attribution.


Other changes can reach further into your privacy program. If a new tool collects or shares customer information, you may need to review your privacy disclosures and determine whether that system affects how you handle consumer privacy requests.


The specific obligations depend on your data practices and applicable privacy laws. But the operational takeaway is straightforward: when you change how customer data moves through your business, it's worth reviewing the privacy workflows connected to it.


## The BFCM changes worth a second look


Some of the most common BFCM updates can affect privacy workflows in ways that aren't immediately obvious. Three situations are particularly worth paying attention to.


### When someone adds another tracking tool


Your agency updates GTM to support a new advertising campaign. The new tag is published, the campaign is ready, and everyone moves on.


But who checked whether the tag was accounted for in your existing consent configuration?


A new tag may load independently of the controls already in place, depending on how it's implemented. It may also introduce a vendor or data flow that hasn't been reflected in your privacy records.


This is why knowing which tags are installed matters just as much as knowing whether they're collecting the data marketing expects.


### When the storefront gets an update


Your ecommerce team launches a seasonal Shopify theme with updated product pages, promotional banners, and new conversion features. The storefront looks good, everything is working, and the team is ready for holiday traffic.


But changes to themes and templates can also affect how tracking and consent-related scripts load. Depending on the implementation, an existing script could be omitted from a new template or behave differently alongside other integrations.


That means a successful storefront launch doesn't necessarily confirm that your consent setup is still working as intended.


When the storefront changes, it's worth making sure the privacy functionality that worked before the update still works afterward.


### When a new vendor becomes part of the customer journey


Maybe you've added a personalization app to recommend products or a promotional tool to capture more holiday sales.


Depending on how it's configured, that tool may collect customer information or share it with another provider. That can affect your vendor records, privacy disclosures, and potentially your consumer request workflows.


For example, if customer information is now stored in another system, the person handling a deletion request needs to know that system exists and whether it should be included in the response.


The more useful question is what customer data the new tool handles, where that information goes, and whether your existing privacy processes account for it.


## Give your privacy setup the same attention as your campaigns


Chances are, you already have privacy tools, policies, and processes in place. As BFCM approaches, the priority is making sure they still reflect how your storefront and marketing stack operate today.


That conversation can happen alongside the campaign and storefront reviews your team is already having.


Marketing knows which tracking tools and advertising integrations have changed. Your ecommerce team and developers know what's been updated on the storefront. And whoever owns privacy or legal compliance can help determine whether those changes affect consent, disclosures, or consumer request workflows.


The important thing is making sure those changes reach the right people and that someone is responsible for coordinating any necessary follow-up.


A good place to start is with three questions:


1. What changed across our storefront, marketing tools, and vendors?
2. Could those changes affect how we collect, share, or manage customer data?
3. Who needs to review or address those implications before BFCM?
